extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists, naturalists, and educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing, judging, and reporting short scientific items (book reviews, letters, expedition notes, technical notes) for a general scientific journal. Covers scientific-method criteria, editorial submission rules, technical-method standards (photography, measurement), and qualities sought in review pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial correspondence submission policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Editor does not hold himself responsible for opinions expressed by correspondents; he cannot undertake to return, or to correspond with, the writers of rejected manuscripts; no notice is taken of anonymous communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should not submit anonymous communications; expect non-return of rejected manuscripts and little or no correspondence on rejected pieces. This is a procedural requirement affecting how letters/manuscripts are submitted and handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of a practical health/self-help book
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful addition to knowledge if it tells how to maintain health and vigour under modern conditions, deals with almost every phase of daily life (food, drink, fatigue, sleep, exercise, baths, physiological states) in an attractive and masterly style that everyone can understand and benefit from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice should be comprehensive across daily life domains, presented clearly and accessibly; moral exhortation alone is insufficient—persistence in public teaching can gradually integrate useful practices into daily life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Botanical guide criteria (Flowers of the Field)
rubrics_metrics.description: A field guide should be adapted for amateur collectors, maintain strengths of older editions while updating taxonomy, augment descriptions, and add good coloured plates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain useful original form when revising; revise species arrangements where necessary; retain guiding headlines under large genera; ensure sufficient size and number of cuts (illustrations); avoid introducing spelling/taxonomic mistakes (examples: 'aureole', 'Hiberna', 'paralias'); good coloured plates should reproduce drawings well and not be 'scrappy and attenuated'. Possession of older editions may still satisfy some botanists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyclopedia usefulness for practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: A cyclopedia of agriculture should divide the continent into sensible districts with chapters by writers specially acquainted with each locality and include practical chapters on planning, stocking, and equipment of farms with capital requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include practical, locality-specific advice useful for practitioners; machinery articles should be serviceable to foreign readers when practices differ; soil and fertiliser chapters can be textbook-like, but avoid overly general essays (e.g., meteorology) that do not encourage intelligent personal study; illustrations should be relevant and not inserted merely to fill space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of seed-germination/root-activity experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments investigating germination/root activation must control water content, prevent re-inoculation from the air, use duplicates, and compare media (earth vs sand) and heat treatments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure duplicates and concordance; keep water-contents identical across treatments; prevent re-inoculation from air (especially for seeds just below surface); include sterilisation controls for seeds themselves; record timing and total germination percentages across temperature treatments; interpret whether effects are due to bacterial action or chemical changes (e.g., low temperature effects argue against major chemical-change explanations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting effects of soil heating on germination
rubrics_metrics.description: Heating soil to various temperatures can markedly retard or prevent seed germination; low temperatures (e.g., 60°C) can reduce germination rates and delay onset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare multiple heating levels (unheated, 60°, 80°, 95°, 150°, 250°); consider re-inoculation experiments (heated then re-inoculated) to separate bacterial from chemical effects; note differences between earth and sand to assess soil chemistry vs biological factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for reporting biological surveys/expeditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A biological expedition report should document careful collections across multiple lake/locality zones, use appropriate gear (tow-net, low-netting), collect representative flora and fauna, record abundance and diversity, and include physical observations (temperature, depth, water-level changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe sampling methods (where, when, duplicate samples), note which groups are present in abundance vs scarce (e.g., copepods abundant, phyto-plankton scarce), record collecting sources (native fishermen) and measures of sizes/weights of specimens; report unexpected presences (e.g., medusa) and notable absences (crabs, prawns, sponges) and provide possible ecological/historical explanations (fresh vs brackish water). Include temperature ranges and vertical gradients with specific readings to explain ecological findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atomic-weight determination by electrolysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine atomic weight electrolytically by direct comparison with a standard (silver), performing multiple determinations and reporting the mean (example: mean of fifteen determinations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, compare elements directly (e.g., cobalt and nickel) by placing multiple voltameters in series and passing the same current; watch for unexpected secondary reactions (noted for nickel) that can invalidate results; support findings with complementary methods (e.g., absorption comparisons for radiation). Provide experimental details later when complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-colour reproduction principle for natural colours
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural colours are imitated by tints in three-colour processes; the accuracy of imitation depends on dye choice, emulsion colour-sensitiveness, and any compensating screen to reduce excessive sensitivity to more refrangible light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that 'natural' reproduction is an approximation by tints visible under suitable light; adjust dye selection and emulsion sensitivity (possibly with a compensating screen) to balance colour rendition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface-grain mosaic requirement for single-plate colour plates
rubrics_metrics.description: For a single plate to contain all three colours, its surface must be divided among the three colours into patches so small that they are not distinguishable to the unaided eye—comparable to woodcut lines or photomechanical dots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure patches are uniformly small and comparable so they blend visually; the three-colour mosaic must be an integral part of the plate (not a separate viewing screen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour proportioning to neutral grey
rubrics_metrics.description: The three colours in the coloured-grained screen must be proportioned so that their combined general impression is a neutral grey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix the red, green, and violet dyed granules in proportions that avoid any colour predominating, producing a visually neutral base for accurate colour reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of a three-colour starch-granule screen
rubrics_metrics.description: Use fairly uniform starch granules dyed separately red, green, and violet; mix thoroughly in correct proportions; spread on glass as a single layer; fill interstices by pressing/crushing the grains (an improvement over filling with black pigment); varnish and apply a specially sensitised emulsion on top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select uniform granules, ensure thorough mixing, apply as one layer, crush to fill gaps rather than using black pigment, varnish before emulsion application. Present the glass side to the lens so light passes through granules first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure and compensation for emulsion orthochromatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Expose the plate with a suitable colour screen at the lens so red, green, and violet lights act upon the emulsion in correct proportions despite the emulsion's lack of orthochromatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a lens-mounted colour screen during exposure and orient the plate with the glass side towards the lens to ensure each stained granule filters light appropriately before it reaches the sensitive layer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal-development procedure for single-plate transparencies
rubrics_metrics.description: After development the negative image must be reversed into a positive by dissolving the metallic silver image with an acid oxidising solution instead of ordinary fixing, then reducing remaining silver bromide to metallic state with a developer; intensification may be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not fix in the ordinary way; use an oxidising acid to remove the developed silver, then redevelop the residual silver bromide. Be prepared to use intensification steps and note the extra trouble relative to simple fixing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical trade-offs of single-plate colour method
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-plate colour plates are comparatively costly but require only one plate (versus several in other methods); reversal is more trouble than simple fixing; results are granulated (grain) whereas other methods yield grain-free images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise cost and grain trade-offs; do not claim practical advantage until plates have been widely tried in actual use; expect future usefulness or modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy of measurement standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate and minute measurement, and patient long-continued labour in sifting numerical results, are often the means by which the grandest discoveries of science are achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value meticulous measurement over superficially lofty pursuits; give measurement prominence in scientific education and public funding priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties and maintenance of physical standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'standard' kept as a physical rod or copied object is fallible: a copy cannot be a real standard because human-made artifacts are liable to error; standards change with temperature and probably with age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design measurement standards and protocols that account for thermal expansion and ageing; recognise that custody and replication of standards require methods that limit changes (temperature control, calibration procedures), not mere physical copies.
